content: Prevalence is a metric used to quantify the frequency of a disease by counting the total number of existing cases within a specific population during a defined time period. Since it is a proportion, prevalence is typically expressed as a percentage of the population. Prevalence rates for particular diseases are calculated using periodic health examination surveys conducted by government agencies. Annual changes in prevalence, as reported in this context, only reflect changes in the population size or composition; the rates themselves do not change unless new survey data becomes available. Therefore, any evaluation of changes in prevalence rates requires data from updated surveys. Point prevalence refers to the proportion of a population that is affected by a disease at a single, specific point in time. It is often described as a snapshot of disease frequency at a particular moment. Period prevalence, on the other hand, measures the proportion of a population that is affected by a disease over a specified duration of time. Unlike point prevalence, period prevalence accounts for cases that were present at the beginning of the time period as well as new cases that developed during that time. This is considered more of a series of snapshots over a continuous time frame rather than a single moment. Period prevalence is also expressed as a ratio or percentage. A common example is a 12-month prevalence, which is often used alongside lifetime prevalence. Point prevalence can also be calculated for shorter, more specific time frames, such as a single month or less. Additionally, there is a related concept called lifetime morbid risk, which represents the theoretical prevalence of a disease at any point in an individual’s life, regardless of the time of assessment. Prevalence calculations rely on two critical assumptions. First, the numerator, which represents the number of existing cases of the disease, must include all currently living cases, regardless of when the disease began. Second, the denominator, which represents the total population, must include everyone in the studied population, encompassing those who are sick, healthy, at risk, and not at risk. As a proportional measurement, prevalence values can only range between 0 and 1, or equivalently, 0% to 100%.
